blocks.x: I'll make a note that the date is March the 22nd, 1962, and we're interviewing Mr. Glass over at 731 St. Peter's Street. And do you mind giving your full name, Henry Glass?
I'm not sure we got that last remark about the, it was over there on the Elation Fields, the Smoky Mary when you used to get the train on.
Yeah, the Fulcher train.
Smoky Mary.
They tell me there'd be a dozen bands over there waiting to get out on the lake sometimes.

That's right. They'd all be sitting right there waiting. Standing right there. Louie Morgan used to be the barroom there. Louie Morgan, he was the captain. Yeah. Morgan, he was the captain on the police force.
It was the barroom out of the lake.
Yeah, no, his barroom used to be right there in the field of Claiborne when you catch the train. When you catch the train, no I didn't know.
He was the captain of the police force.
Yeah, he was the captain of the police force. Louie Morgan. Bucko Lager, he used to be at, he was the barber. Yeah. On Frenchman Street. Frenchman in Claiborne.
Bucko played baritone. Bucko Lager.
No, that's Bucko, you talking about Bucko. I'm talking about Bucko Grandma. Bucko Grandma. No, Bucko Grandma. Bucko used to play too with us. Bucko Grandma, he did.
How many cars did they have on that train, that Smokey Mary train?
Sometimes, oh when she had five cars, that was a big dip, big picnic, you know, like on a Sunday she'd use five cars. Use five of them.
Several bands.

Several bands. Several bands. Yeah, all through the week she'd have, well you see, the white people would be in the front coaches, you see, and the college would be all in the back coaches. Sometimes it'd be two coaches or-
They had separate coaches. Yeah, yeah, separate coaches.
Yeah.
I never even thought about that before, that they had segregation on the smoking. Yeah, they had that.
I don't remember if they had segregation, but I mean I'll tell you what happened. If they didn't have much room or enough room, they'd get on there and they'd get anywhere on it.
Get anywhere. Yeah, they'd ride the back some of them.
You got several bands on the same train.
Yeah. All the bands would get in there. They wouldn't believe it. Because them picnets would be in between with them bands, you know. We'd be going to play for them people at camps.
And you remember any other places? You mentioned fish fries you played for and-
Oh, well, fish fries, well they would be all over. Yeah. Yeah, all over. Sometimes we'd play at the Fry's on the Hall, there would be a big fish fry there.

You know most of the fish fries that people would have in the houses and the yard and just frying the fish and things on the front would be on the fry that night. Yeah. But most of them was Friday night. Friday night. That was a fast night. They'd make fast gumbo and fish and potato salad. Then later on it started Saturday night.

And you see they'd put a red deer, you could tell anywhere a fish fry was going to be, they'd have a red lantern hanging out. Oh, somebody told me that one. Yeah, they'd have a lantern hanging out over the gate. I got one of them lanterns wrong. Yeah, they'd red in the bankage, you know, and they'd have that red lantern.
You could tell. Right, that's not red. All they used to do was red in the glass.
Yeah, like the ones they put out when they repair the street with little oil.
Yeah, they'd hang up like a lamp. In other words, people sometimes would use it in the house, the white ones, not the red ones.
As long as you could hang it on something. Yeah, I think I've seen that. Put a stick out there, yeah. Yeah. If the globe wouldn't be red, they'd take and tie a red rag around.
I had one in my locker. I think the globe was dropping and broke the globe. I'd just keep them, you know.
Were those sticks dry mostly inside the house or would some of them be out in the yard?

In the yard, out in the yard and inside. Like a lawn party? Yeah, lawn party. I've gone to a couple of lawn parties. Lawn parties and things like that, yeah. Anywhere there's anything like that, wasn't in the hall, they'd have that lantern out. Yeah. That way you'd know whether something was going on there.
Yeah, two trees in one block at some time, you know. You'd smell the fish. Yeah.
Or you'd smell the fish riding the red beans and gumbo. You'd smell it. Cowan dinner.
When you'd play with just the piano player, who were some of the piano players around in those days that you worked with, if you can remember?
Can you remember some of them?
No, I'm trying to study. I don't want to tell you the old ones, because these young fellas.
They're the ones you used to play with.
Yeah, I'm telling you about the old fellas. Most of the older men that were interested in hearing about that early history, since it's a history project we're working on. Well, they are.
I used to play with Walter Deco sometimes. Yeah, Walter played. Walter Deco.

Them were the, well, them piano players. Most any fellas would come up and play piano. You understand? Did they know many pieces, or just a couple of blues? Oh yeah, well there's the blues. They didn't want nothing but the blues. When you play the piano in the supper, they wanted the blues singing like High Long and all different things like that, you know. It was more the blues. Stagger Lee and Billy Lyon and all that. That's all they would. Well any of them fellas would come up and get in there. See, there wasn't no local. Well sometimes the fellas would come up and wouldn't have a piano player. And the fellas would be passing there and just stop in and just beat a drum. Piano player wouldn't show up. I used to see Harold Santiago.
You see?
You just had to walk around and you'd get a job. As long as you could beat any kind of nobody.

And some of them stuff was playing. Harold Santiago, he never played out of much for money, but he used to like good time and stuff. Yeah, he enjoyed playing for them. Yeah, blacks brother. Blacks brother. Yeah, I know.
He's old brother.

Yeah, the fellas, they just passed there and stopped in, gone to play. It wasn't worrying about the money. As long as they were getting something to drink and eating, they'd play in, plenty of women there now. That's how them supper would go. Sometimes the people would get the piano player, sometimes women would be in there, could play the piano for the time of the distance, you know. We had women do it all around.
Did you ever work in any of the dance halls in the district, much that you can remember?

Well, I played in two, three places. Played on Villery and Benville. I played in the back of the ballroom, the saloon there. Played back there. Played on St. Louis. Who ran that place on Villery and Benville?
Do you remember who ran that place?
Old fella, they used to call him Papa, I believe. He had some daughters, Papa.
So the back room of the saloon, did they have dancing there? Yeah, we did. Do you remember the entertainers there? It was on Franklin Street, what they call Crozat now, I guess.
Do you remember anything about the entertains, the hummingbirds, Black and Tans? No. I don't know. A few dance halls.
I understand in the very old days they didn't have many dance halls in the district at first, but that is where they had a whole band.
Yeah, we had the Columny Hall. Oh yeah.
Yeah, the Columny Hall.

That ain't the district. No, it was Irsaline. I was down in the Oisaline. We had the Poise of Viernes Hall. We had the Frasier Me Hall. But they're still there now. Yeah, they're still there. The Poise of Viernes Hall. The church now, they made a church at the Poise of Viernes. Well that's nice. Because of me it's a church too, I think. Yeah, I used to belong to all them societies there, the Poise of Viernes. We had the Poise of Viernes. We used to band music too. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They had died out. Even the artesian hall, they tore down.
Yeah, the artesian hall, yeah.
Yeah, it's torn down. Yeah.
And the new hall is still over there, but that's apartments and the people living in there.
George Amie. George Amie is still on Robinson Street.

Yeah, he made some records there last year. Now, Teesham Hall, they tore that down. The Undertaker's there on Durban Street. A year ago, about two years now. Did you get any pictures of that? Oh yeah, I had some pictures. I recorded Wooden Joe there.
Yeah. Old Big Al Louie, he died. He was staying right back there. I know, he's going to stay. Yeah, he stayed right there.
Yeah, I took some pictures when he was living there.
Yeah, I used to go get him all the time. We used to go all over and play around there, you know.
Speaking of Big Al, can you tell us any other clarinetists you worked with? Do you remember, did you say something about the Teos a minute ago? Did you heard him when you were young?

Teo, Leo Teo. No, I never played with him. Teo, what I was trying to tell you about, that was the fellow for Warline. He used to have Mr. Fred Tudry. He used to run the piano store for Warline. Yeah, I'm not sure. Fred Tudry and them. Yeah, that was relation to the Carreras. Dr. Tudry and them. All that's relation. Gladys Carreras and all them.

Do you remember old man Cottrell, Louis Cottrell's father, the guitar player who was the, I think he worked for Warline's too. Yeah. And picking out drums for him and things sometimes, at least test them out for him. Do you remember how he played? Anything about him much on the street or how? It was pretty good.
Well, you were good. One of the best actors. Yeah, you. How are you?
Hi, you're early. Yeah, you're early. Hour late, you sir. You're early. Hour late.
They understood us to be 7 o'clock.
Okay, you've already finished it, huh?
No, no, we're just getting a good start. We were late started. Okay, come on. We've got another 20 minutes left here on this reel. If you've got a few questions, you'll be fine.
Sure, I've got some. Okay, what about Djalma Gagne? Did you cover that?
No, I haven't found his son yet.
Did you talk about Djalma Gagne yet? Yeah.
Yeah, Gagne.
No, you never, you say your player originally.

Well, Djalma used to be the leader of our band. What band? Well, he was with, for the buzzards. When you had the camellia band? Yeah, when he was carrying the camellia band. I let him carry the camellia band. He was a leader. Yeah, I let him lead.
And who was in that band?
Well, Bucko Grammar.
Grammar is his name?
Yeah, Bucko Grammar. What did he play? He played baritone. George Foyer played bass tuba. George?
George Foyer.
That poor boy.
He played bass tuba.
And all that's dead. Bob Anthony played trumpet. I know him.
Is he dead now? No, I don't know him.
From your little Bob Anthony? Yeah, little Bob Anthony. Hospital in Velocity. Yeah, Bob played trumpet with us. Archie Robinson played trombone. Rene Moikadel.
Rene Moikadel. Rene Moikadel.
Rene Moikadel. Rene Moikadel. He played what?
Saxophone. Saxophone. No. Who's playing trombone, you remember? Archie Robinson and Joe Petit. Yeah, Joe Petit played with us. You must have had some trumpet players.
Oh yeah, we had good trombone. You had Dejama Garnier. Yeah, you were good. Who else? Garnier and who else? Garnier, Wooden Joe, and Bob Anthony.
Bob Anthony. And Bob Anthony. Mm-hmm. And Bob Anthony. And Bob Anthony. And Bob Anthony. And Bob Anthony. And Bob Anthony.
Yeah, he was good. Yeah, he was good.
Yeah, he was good.

And we had Archer Robinson on trombone. Who was playing? Eddie Summon. Eddie Summon was playing trombone. Sometime. Sometime after then. Yeah, sometime after that, yeah. Eddie Summon. And I forget this album. Albert Francis. Albert Francis was playing snare drum. Albert Francis played snare drum. I was playing bass. And Boybanks used to play clarinet. And Boybanks used to play clarinet.
Yeah.
You all had a good lineup. Oh yeah, we had a good lineup. How often did y'all play?
Oh, we used to play for the buzzards and things.

We'd get to the buzzards and things. We'd get to the rhythm for the carnival, you know? Round for the carnival time. That's when we played at brass band. That's when we played at brass band. And we'd play the bass. And I was playing bass. And Boybanks used to play clarinet. Yeah. You all had a good lineup. Oh yeah, we had a good lineup. How often did y'all play? Oh, we used to play for the buzzards and things. We'd get to the rhythm for carnivals, you know? Round for carnival time. That's when we played at brass band. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Then I took the chamella band.

That's why we named them to chamella band because I was carrying the chamella band after johnny I was carrying the Camellia Band, the orchestra. Garnier was carrying the brass band, Camellia Band, you understand? We made it go to Camellia.
You know Wilbur Tillman? Did you ever play with him?
Tillman, yeah, I played with Tillman.
What band did he play with?
I just remember, I believe Tillman was playing with the Excelsa Band.
Yeah. You mean did Tillman play with the Tuxedo? Yeah. Wilbur, yeah.
Yeah. Excelsa Band.
What was he playing? What was he playing? What instrument then?
He was playing drums. Well that's a different Tillman.

No, you're talking about a different Tillman. Yeah, he was playing drums. He was talking about the Tillman that played with John Kasman, John Kasman's cousin. Oh no, no, no. You never played with him. No. You played with him with John. Maybe that's Cornelius Tillman? Did you ever know Cornelius Tillman? I didn't know his other name, I just know him by Tillman. Oh, I see. He played with Wilbur, with John Kasman. Yeah. Well what about, did you ever play with Big Al-Louis?
Yeah. I was like, Big Al-Louis to be my clarinet player. With what band?
The Chamelea Band.
So you play in the brass band or the dance band?
He played in the brass band too. Both, huh?
Yeah, he played parades too with us. He played for the Budsets a couple of times. What about Didi? Didi? Didi, trumpet player. He played with John too?
Yeah, Didi used to be the leader.
After Dejan McConaughey. Yeah.
After he died.
Yeah. After he died.
Yeah, Didi used to be the leader there. That's right. The trumpet player. I remember when he was playing with John. Yeah.
Little Cag. Little Cag used to work with John. Cag didn't work with John much. Lawrence Tucker worked with John.
Yeah, Lawrence Tucker. Yeah, Lawrence Tucker.
Yeah, Lawrence Tucker. Cag. The D.
Bob Astley. They played with John more than after. Yeah, more than now.
After Kanye died, they played with John more than now. Yeah. More than now. More than in . Yeah.
More than in . Know much about . Know much about . The D, Bob Adler, they played with Charles Moreland. Yeah, Moreland and Manila. After Kanye died, they played with Charles Moreland and...
Moreland and Keg and him.

That's right. Well, what about this guy? Did you talk about your teacher any? Did you have a teacher? What's his name? Edward Gaspar had that. You got that. Yeah, he got that. We got some more. Who is Edward Gaspar?
Edward used to be a snare drum player, you know? I'd just be playing around there. He'd come and learn me.
I see. Well, who did he play with?
He used to play with this boy, Walter Blue. They had an orchestra, you know? Yeah. Well, I used to go around and follow them around, and I'd pick up playing Black Benny.
And you said you got your bass drum inspiration from Black Benny. Yeah.

Black Benny, that's where I took up them. Black Benny, I used to follow them, you know, with the parades. Who did Black Benny play with? Black Benny used to play, I don't remember what the band Black Benny was playing with. He'd just give the name of the band behind the fellas which was playing, you know, the leader. Oh yeah.
Who would get the job.
You see, the fellas would get the job, they'd call it their band, you know?
Like Buddy PT.
I used to play with Buddy PT. Well, we called it Buddy PT's band. I played with Chris Kelly, well, we called it Chris Kelly's band. You see, the one with the leader, we called that their band.
Were those reading bands, or were they more on the tunk brass band style of them? Just right, the tunk band.
It was a regular tunk band.
Yeah, yeah.
There wasn't no reading bands.
What clubs would they play for?
Well we'd play for them fuelings, like the Charity and the Liberty and things like that. They'd play them.
Did you talk about the Moreiros? Did you play with the band? Lawrence Morello?
Yeah, I used to play with Lawrence. Lawrence used to play bands in the band with us.
You talked about that before?
No, we hadn't talked about Lawrence.
Well who was Lawrence with? What band?

Lawrence was playing with the Camellia band, with me. Archer Robinson was playing trammol. Well you see, the same fella we'd use on them brass bands, we'd take and use them out for the orchestra. I see.
And what about your bass player with Lawrence? Who was the bass player?
We'd use slow drag sometimes. T. Ruscha.
Did you use any of his other brothers, or his daddy, or anybody like that? One two.
Joe Doyard used to play trumpet with us. I don't know him. You didn't know he was there.

How'd it come back? You met his brother, Wilfred? His son. Oh no, I introduced Wilfred to you or somebody out there. No, not me. Wilfred Doyard was out there. Who I introduced him? To Ralph. Yeah, one of them, they were so sad. He lived down there, we can go there sometime whenever you want, or Two Road Street. I know where he lived. Yeah. What about Billy Moran? Billy Moran. Did you ever work with him?
I worked with Billy Moran.
What band was that?
Well they were going to the Excelsior Band, Billy Moran.
You ever play with John Morrero or this other? Yeah, John, yeah.
I played with Lawrence Morrero, brother John, and then he was playing bass. He was playing bass, John. I was trying to get him to play bass now.
Oh, who is this guy George Stewart? George Stewart? Yeah, the clarinet player. Yeah, he did, yeah. Is he dead or alive or was he dead?
I believe George Stewart dead, I don't know what you're talking about. George Bendy and I.
George Stewart just played for the Alibaba, and that's a regular job.
He was slim like George Lewis. He just was slim like George Lewis.
And who did he play with? What band? I didn't get that.

Well he used to work with all the bands, you know. He'd work in with the Camellia Band, Excelsior, he'd work anywhere. You see that's the way they'd hire the fellas, all in between. It's like how all the fellas, they know how all that's good, they'd get him. You see you have to pick out your best mans to go out on these street parades and things like that. And that's how we worked it.
Bill, did you get who some of the people you heard when he was young? We asked a few.

Yeah, who were some of the bands you heard when you just were getting interested in music? Do you remember the name of some of the bands? When you were quite young, you know, some of the musicians you liked?

Well I liked a lot of them. I liked all the bands. Because I just was wild over the music. I liked Ambrose and all them fellas like that, and it was all older bands than me. And I just come up with them. Ambrose was a banjo player? Yeah, Ambrose was all in me when I started playing. Ambrose what?
Which one?
Ambrose, he used to play banjo. I got him confused.
Now is it Ambrose that played trombone? Ambrose played trombone.
Two different guys? Yeah.
Two different guys? Yeah.

He played trombone and one played banjo. Ambrose made him a banjo, he had a banjo made out of one of them cheese box. He'd make his banjo. Who did he play with? Well he was playing with Johnny Predos and them. Wooden Joe. Well they just would move around.
But he would play that funny little banjo, that homemade banjo on a real band? Yeah, on a real band.

He made it. It was made. I didn't know if I could get my hand on it. I'm going to find out from some of these people that they got that banjo. It's made out of cheese box. He glued that and made it and put heads on it. It was a banjo too. I'd love to see it. You could hear that baby, you could hear that baby. Yeah, he made it. Now just like Noone had made that horn, he used to slide. Kazooka. That kazooka, he was made there.
Did you go uptown to hear many bands in downtown?
No, I always went around. That's when I'd go play, you know, like that.
But when you were a little boy you didn't go to different sections?

No. That's when they'd come and get me to play, you see. Because Dr. Tudray had raised me, you see, and I just got out. Like that, Lysian Field and Claiborne, that's who adopted me, Dr. Tudray. Well I started playing when I was 21 years old. And I got out. I went to play music. And I just took a liking to it and I just, I got it up and there.
But guys, Buddy Bowling, did you ever hear him? I heard Buddy Bowling.

That was an old band. I thought I heard Buddy Bowling, but you see, fuck you, motherfucker. I heard all that. Yeah, I didn't know them. Them was all old men, you see. Them men way before my time. I was coming up. I was about that size when Buddy Bowling and them was playing. They had a band, Warner in them, Warner Reed.
What did he play?
Warner Reed and Tatee. There was two brothers. They played bass. One played bass and one played banjo. Warner played which? One played bass and one played banjo.
Which played which, though?
Well Warner played bass and Tatee played the banjo. And we had Bob Woodley.
Remember Bob Woodley?

Bob was a little short dumb fella. Bob used to play ghetto. We called him Bob Woodley. I never heard of him before. I don't know a thing about him. Yeah. Bob Woodley. Was he? Yeah, he was good. Did he have his own band, Bob Woodley? No. Bob Woodley and them used to work with Juan in them.
You know. He used to work with Juan in them. He used to work with me.
For me. For me. For me.
For me. For me.
For me.
For me. For me.
For me. For me. For me. He used to call it Tate and Warner's band.
Who was that violin player? Wasn't that violin player named Tate? No. Sales? I'm going to come over here and see you. What about Buddy Lock? Did you ever hear Buddy Lock?
No, I never heard.
I thought that was a bass button. Let me see, who else I was going to ask you about? Those bands like Warner and Tate.
Them were supposed to be big bands. They were supposed to be the best bands coming up in that time. How many pieces? They'd have four pieces.
And they'd be bass and what, guitar you'd say? Yeah, bass.
And what else?
And trumpet.
And drums.
And drums. Drums. They used drums when you first started? Oh yeah. They had drums.
Yeah, they used drums.
They had two drums or one drum?

Two drums. Bass drums. We had our drums, we had a strap, our pedal, our foot pedal was a strap that come from over here. See, you'd press down on it and hit that bass drum with that strap and it had a big ball on the middle there. See, you'd pull that strap.
You say you got a look you might have one at home.
I might have it at home. I'm going to look around. It's an old trap.
Oh, who were you playing with when the September storm hit here? In September?

We were Johnny Predoss. That's in 1950. Yeah, the Camellia band. I was playing with the Camellia band. And you must have stayed with them for a while. I did stay with Johnny. I stayed with Johnny. Those used to work from one place to the other, from one band to the other. Fellas would hire me when Johnny didn't have nothing. They'd come in hire me. That's just like the fellas do now, you know? What about when the Depression hit?
Who were you with? In the Depression? Yeah.

I was playing for myself in the Depression. I was working for myself. I'd get out there and work and unload cold cars. I'd catch a job playing, go to the lake or something like that, you know? And I'd play them picnics. You still unload them cold cars? I'd unload gondola cars by myself. I unload two a day by myself. One at night and one in the day. I'd unload it for George Kelly. I'd wheel it out. I was only making $10 a car. $10? That's all I made. Them big gondolas. Them big gondolas. I'd unload one in the day and one at night. I'd go to the union building and throw one over for Mr. Dillman. I'd throw one over the fence, slack, you know? Throw a car slack out by myself. And I'd wheel a car cold over with a big wheelbar.
Wheel it over the fence.
Enough of the work you do now.
And you'd play music at night?
I'd play music. I'd be calm, I'd play music. If I didn't have nothing to do, I'd go play music. If anybody would come for me.
That man carry a heart right now.

Yeah, I've been working hard all my day. Hard work don't kill you. I've been working hard all my day. I'd get in the gravel car and throw one out by myself. And I can tell you this was the time I could unload one. I'd get in the gravel car for six o'clock, and four thirty of that evening, I'd throw that gravel car out by myself.
I'm glad it's you, not me.
Ain't going to miss you, look at the clock, when I get in there. And for four thirty I'd be and throw that car gravel out.
Did you ever play music in church?
Well yeah, I played a couple of churches. Sunday school, picnics and things like that, you know? They played for the picnics, you know, on the Sunday school ground.
What religion are you?
I'm Baptist.
And you play for the Baptist church sometimes?
Yeah. They have Sunday school picnics, you know. We go out there and play.
Many of the dance musicians ever play in church too? Oh yeah.
I play churches now. Right during the services? I play, not in the service. We play in the back of the halls and things, you see the ground there.

Dick, if I'm not mistaken, I think that's where Rubelow met his wife. Sure, we play churches. Oh, in this Rubelow? Yeah. Played playing in the church. I used to hear Remus Matthews in the church here, you know? Sure. And what's his name, Harrison Barnstone, when he played in church? Since lately the preachers, the young preachers now, they don't want that.

We made supper and things, and we'd have the band back there playing church hymns and things like that, you know, back there. That's how it was. It's music right on. Sure. Though we were playing church hymns, you know? Like when the saints go marching in over in the glory land, just to close to walk with thee. Play all that. Lord, Lord, you certainly been good to me and all kinds. There's all different, like them spiritual hymns and things. We played all that. I played in the sanctified churches too. Played there.
Now that's where you get some.
You get out there and go around one of them sanctifieds, then you get some records. Oh yeah. I don't know what that is. They tear them down.
They don't call that dancing though, do they? No.
No, they be dancing though. They be Lindenhopping . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm . Mm-hm .
They don't call that dancing though, do they?

No. No they be dancing though. They be Lindnerhopping. I don't think they know. Yeah they be Lindnerhopping. Yeah they can do that bopping. Like what we call the, what do they call it, the Popeye? Well they be Popeye too.
I've seen them doing all kind of stuff in Jersey.
I'm telling you. You been to a Sanctified church? I've been there.
They do it. They do it. Just a feeling for a record?

It's calling out a band. The rhythm the band put there get more rhythm on them. You put the rhythm to them and they can go. And you make them happy too. I get on that bedroom and make them happy. It's just the spirit they get. The swing.
Who do you think invented that wire beater for the cymbal? You know, the beater that gives it the- What I got? Who's the first one to ever make that?
Well I seen Black Banner with that.
Before anybody else?
Yeah I seen Black Banner with that. I made one. I made that. And put the cymbal on the top of it.
What did the other drummers use?

Did they have anything like that? No, some of them didn't. I never seen them with it. But they started using it now, you know? Because that answers for the music, you have to have that cymbal, that brass. Some of the other bands, they'd have two cymbals. They'd have a band, they'd have them two cymbals slapped together. They'd have a man just to play that cymbal.
In other words they made that to take the place of a man.
Yeah, it may take the place of a man, you see?
You ever see a two-handed bass drummer down here? Yeah.
We have them school band there. The school band, that's what they're using now. All the school just playing that two-hand with the bass drum.
But the old timers didn't do that?

No, no. This is new, the schools coming up with this is new. Now, I can do what they do with that, with that, them two hands, I can take that, take my one hand on that beater, and that cymbal and do this what they're doing.
You double-dipping. Oh yeah, I can do that.
Working two jobs.
Yeah, I can do that.
Of course, well it looks like it's cutting a man out, you know? It's in order.
What do you think Buddy got his style of playing? Buddy Petit I'm talking about.

Buddy Petit got his, learned right there on St. Anthony and Robinson. From whom? I didn't know who he learned it from. I know he used to sit down there all day, half of the night, blowing right there, Robinson and St. Anthony, the old corner house. I know when Buddy Petit was learning. I just thought. His first wife was named Lizzy.
Buddy Petit. I thought maybe he had somebody there who might have given him a few little tips on how to make all that stuff.
No, I used to just see him there by himself. He'd be blowing there. Working out himself?
Working out himself.
He's a blues player too. Chris Keller was a blues player too. Who else played good blues?
Well, Louis Armstrong used to be good too. He was a good blues player. Do you really think he's good?
Oh yeah. I know he's good. I know he's good. I know he's good. Louis come from the home. From Jones home. Many of them did.
Yeah. Jones is throwing a lot of good trumpet players out there now.

Gooder than that. Yeah, every day. Thomas Chappison. Thomas Chappison. Yeah. Now Bichet was lying right around my house clarinet. And Paul Bond was lying right at my house with a flute. One of them little silver flutes, them little flutes, them little flutes, and they were little silver flutes, them little flutes. Which kind?
The kind? You hold straight out in front of them? Yeah.
The little bit of flutes. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
I thought he was dead. He is dead. I'm going to get his picture for you. His photograph.
His wife told me she's going to give it to me.
Raymond Glapion. Let's see, what reel is this? Is this reel three? Reel three, yeah. Henry Glass, better known as Booker T, huh? Yeah.

You tell him how you got your nickname? Yeah, Dr. Tudrick gave me that name, Lindsey Phil Claymore. He's ready. He just thought called you Booker T. Let's give me, well you see, he's got a name. He's got a name. He's got a name.
He's got a name.
He's got a name. He's got a name.
He's got a name. He's got a name. Lindsey Phil Claymore. He's ready.
He just thought called you Booker T.

Well you see, they're around Lindsey Phil and Claymore, they didn't allow them colored fellas to be around there. I was the only colored fellas used to hang up around there because I would come up there and I would work them by Dr. Tudrick, you know. I stayed there. But when them colored fellas would come around there, they'd be fighting and going on, they'd be running them. Well I was the only colored fellas. I'd be in a gang with the white fellas, they'd have to run them too, you know. Though when they'd do me something, you see when they'd do me something, I'd get the stick and I'd beat them. You see when I'd whip them, I'd run hard. The white boy, Louis Morgan there, he was the copper, captain of the police force. And he'd say, where Booker T. at? I'd run and hide in the system. Dr. Tudrick had a big system, you know, with the brick around the system. I'd get up in that system, I'd stay there and tell him Dr. Tudrick. But when they'd come look for me, I wouldn't come out. Dr. Tudrick would come and he'd call me when I'd come out. I'd know he was there. Nobody wasn't going to do me nothing. He'd go, Booker, what you done? I said, I didn't do nothing. He said, well Booker didn't do nothing. He said, because Booker never tell a lie. I used to sit in the middle of the table there. Yeah, I'd whip them with a stick. Yeah, I'd whip them with a stick, you see. My words went before them boys, because you know I wouldn't fight them if they didn't do me something. And I'd fight them all, beat them with a stick. I'd catch them in the head, beat them, throw them on the ground. My name is in that tree at Legend Field and Clayborne. That big tree right on the corner. They got much of concrete in there. My name is written in there. You pay that little. When you were a little boy you did? When I was a boy. I was a boy. I was a devil. Wooden Joe got his fingers cut like that, coming from Mel and Boyd. Well I always wondered, what was that? I knew he had him cut because he was coming from the picnic. He was coming from playing the picnic, about eleven o'clock that night. Him and Lulu Pascal. That was the last train, you know. Him and Lulu Pascal?
Lulu Pascal.
He was coming in. And he was bringing Lulu home. Where Lulu played? Lulu don't play nothing. She was coming, he was bringing her home. She went on the picnic.
Oh, wow, it was his chick.
Yeah, yeah, he was bringing her home, you see. And they got there, them boys was cutting at him and he throwed his hand up. Cut all them fingers. I saved him.
What boys?

Them white boys, the Lindenfield and Claiborne. They call them the twins. There was a bunch of brothers, they called the twins there. They was bad. Well, you saved him, huh? Yeah, I stopped them by me being around there, you see. I told them don't do anything. That was your gang? Yeah, that was all my gang, you see. And I saved Joe and Lulu. They had Lulu piled up in glass bottle. Twenty cases of bottles, empty bottles. They had her between the steps. They had done broke all them bottles, throwing at her. She was standing up in between the steps. They just throwing them, busting them on the pavement at her. They had done run to Joe and cut Joe's fingers almost off. He threw his head. And I saved her. I believe Lulu living yet, Lulu Pascal?

Yeah. Wait, no wait, let me see. After you have Lulu Pascal. I think she's living in Joe Pascal living. Wait a minute. Yeah, they carried him there. I don't know if she's living under that. I mean, I heard that name.
I heard that name. I heard that name. I heard that name.
I heard that name about this about, or not about a mother. Joe Pascal, he's a slater, a roofer.
Do you remember the Spanish and American War? Yeah. Well, I remember the Civil War, too. What went on there? Shooting and gun on.
They had a haul.
They had a haul. They had a haul. They couldn't get them out. They had some shooting.
They had a haul. They had a haul. Spanish and American War? Yeah.
I remember the Civil War too.
What went on then?

Oh, they had a time. They had a battle around from the French Quarter in that time. Shooting and going on. They had a hall. I remember it was on Royal Street or Charter Street there. Couldn't get them out there. They had some shooting that was going on there. Remember that? You heard of it. A lot of shooting was going on there.
Did they have many bands here during that time?
Well, bands like we'd have for fish rides and supper, for the Columnear Hall and things like that. They had bands.
What's a fish ride?

The women used to wear guinea blue dresses and aprils. They were dressed up. When the fella had a pair of overhands and a jumper, you were dressed up. Shoeshine. They had jumpers, shoes, shoeshine, button, jumper with four buttons on each side. The women wear a bonnet with big ruffles on them.
And his watch chains, cross his chest with his father.
Yeah, that's right.
Calico. That's right. And we go to Calico Ball? Yeah, they had that. Guinea blue.

Yeah, we had all that. When we come up, we had short pants. I was 21 years old when I was in short pants. The policemen just run us in short pants. We had them big striped stockings. Thick rib stockings.
Thick rib you see. Big black stockings.
We dressed alike. A jumper and our cap. We dressed up. Jeans pants. The women would wear guinea blue dresses. Plenty ruffles around them. Ruffles all around them. Long dresses though.
Who'd you play your first job for, first music job? The first music job?
The first music job? I played for the stave handlers. Stave handlers?
Yeah. Where was this? On Claiborne. Walter Blue dropped dead that Sunday.

Really? Yeah, that's the time Walter Blue dropped dead. They call themselves the stave handlers. They used to handle, they call them now car unloaders. They unload them cars out on the other side of Jackson Avenue up in there. Handling staves for the make bows. They call themselves the stave handlers. They used to play their parades.
Do you remember who was in that band?
Walter Blue, Edwild Gasper, that's who I was playing with.
Did they have more than one band ever in parades in those times?
No, they had that one band.
When they have a big band, a big parade, how many bands would they have though?

Two bands. You remember Hot Goblins and them like that. They'd have two bands. Who did they hire? Well I wouldn't know all the fellas in the band. You don't know the names of the bands? Because I used to belong to the Hot Goblins and things like that. Yeah, I belonged to the Hot Goblins and the Hot fellas and things. But I wasn't too much of interest in playing with them, you know? Because they had all their own bands, all the older bands in our work. Willie Parker?
Yeah.
I guess Willie Parker was in there.
Yeah, Willie Parker was in there.

He'd play a bass drum. You never would get that picture of Willie Parker? I'm going to go over there and I'm trying to get my picture from Willie Parker. He's got my picture over there. When I was a young man, that's what I wanted to give it to you, when I was screwing Cotton, Cotton Screwman. And I'm trying to get that picture. I'm going to ask him for his picture. I'm more sure he'd give it. I'm going to get Raymond Galapio's picture. His wife told me she'd give it to me. And Willie Phillip's son said he'd give it to me. Well, Joe, you've got one in Joe's picture, huh? Darryl says he has another picture. I just start sending him, then he's going to send me to him. Yeah. Well, he sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He sends him to him. He goes to him to him. He goes to him to him.
He goes to him to him. He goes to him to him.
He goes to him to him.
He goes to him to him to him. Yeah. Yeah. He goes to him to him to him.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
he died a couple years before. Buddy PT, I see son, I might get Buddy PT's.
You know what picture we want, bro? If you can get a picture? Somebody with a picture of Chris Kelly.
All right. I'mma see can I get Chris Kelly's picture. I told him if they take Lil Jack's picture,

just hook a trumpet on it or something. Take it? He saw Lil Jack, look, this image. Just like him, huh? The image. I don't know if he can I get Chris Kelly, let's see who got that picture. You know all the people, that's what I say, you might run across somebody that has that picture. Wooden Joe's people might have Chris's picture.
You never know. If I ain't mistaken, I'd be with Chris Kelly on a picture of Wooden Joe's, how the wife had got there. One of them. I'm sure I seen that picture of Chris Kelly.
You go there and find out? I'mma see. Well what about these different places you played? What were some of the different kind of tonks you were in and halls and everything?
Well I played Calum Hall, and Artesium Hall like that. George and Me, Frater Me Hall, Poison Burns Hall. They were playing in a really tough place?
Oh yeah, they were all good places. I know that Burren and Biennale where you used to play was tough.

Yeah, that was rough there. Where was that? What's that? In the district. In the district there. What was the name of that place? They had a whole fella, they had that place, they called him Papa. Papa's place. I know what I'm going to ask you. Do you remember Farmer
George? Fireman George? He used to have a parade with one colored fireman here, and he'd go out and have a parade himself by himself. Nobody else, just him.

I might don't slip my remembrance, you know. You know all them times, it's been some time. Yeah. I done been through a whole lot. What are they called? Fireman George? Yeah, Fireman George. What are you playing?

He just had a parade. Just one man would have his own parade. I think Louis Armstrong played for him. Well, he had a band to play for him. Yeah, one man would hire a whole band. Oh yeah, that's all right. That's big time. Did you ever play a parade for just one man?
No.
That's a one man club.
Yeah, he didn't want nobody but himself, with himself.
That place Papa's place, huh?
Yeah. Band Run and Bill.
What went on there, were they?
Well, we used to have dancing in the back. I played at Spanos. Spanos, Savoca. Oh yeah? I played in the, that was the dishes, you know.
Well what about Spanos and Savoca? How big a band would they have there?
I have three pieces, four pieces.
Who played at Spanos?
Well I had Walter Blue and all of them. I had Walter Blue. Sometimes I'd have Chris Kelly, Jack Carey. Jack Carey played slide.
Did he play lead when he was there much, or would he play?
Well he was a good trombone. He played the lead? Jack Carey. A good trombone player.
You couldn't have had a big band in those places?
No. Four pieces, three pieces was the most. When you had a four piece band you had a big band.
Yeah. But I know Jack could execute. Yeah. He's good. Would you have the piano players in those places?
Yeah, sometimes they'd have pianos.
Do they have any guys?

You see, your band, when they didn't have a piano, would you use a ghetto? A banjo, you know. We'd use banjo more. Banjo. When they stomp off like that, everybody's come in. That's how we'd give our sign. So now the fellas tell you, we know this what you're going to do, in a brass band.
Did they have many guitar players that would just play with their fingers and wouldn't use a pick ever?
Yeah.
Who would do that?
Bob. He played with his fingers. Had a con there.
Yeah. Would have said that.

Yeah. They'd have a con that play. Some of them fellas use that pick. Some of them would use their, they'd use a little, a little bone. They'd file that bone, a piece of waist bone. They'd file it and they'd get them strings too. Don't think they wouldn't hit them.
Could they make themselves hurt when they used them?
Oh yeah, they could hit them strings. They can get to them, in between them strings.
Yeah, but I mean when they just used their fingers would they make themselves hurt?
Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
Play loud, doesn't it?
Yeah, loud, loud. Yeah, it's good. Well that pick would get up when they were going to put that rhythm, you know, they'd use that pick.
But for solos, what would they use?
They could pick with their fingers. Some of them pick their fingers good. Their fingers would just that hard, you know.
Yeah. Yeah, you can see them have a con on their hands.
Oh yeah. Oh yeah. And they'd hit it with that fingernail, you know. They know how to get to them.
Did they have many guys just walk around playing, just strolling around the street, you know, serenading?

Yeah, they had a lot of them used to come around and just sit down and play for nothing. Just go around the place and play for nothing. Come in the ballrooms and play and they'd play. Like around in the district, they'd just come sit in there and play.
Did you ever know that guy called Doug used to play around the district and went up north?
No.
He played little mandolin and ukulele and stuff like that. Punchy nosey.

I just forget this boy's name. He used to play Kodgen. What did he call it? Old man Ford. He used to play Kodgen. That was a band. They had a Kodgen, a Kodgen and a Washboard. And that was a band. And that was a band. Who played the Kodgen?
I don't know. Did he have a separate guy to do it? Or would Ford play it?
The one who was playing the band, the Washboard. Oh yeah? He'd have that Kodgen. I got one of them little Kodgen home. A little tin Kodgen. That's what he'd play.
If you can play them, all right? They sound real good. Oh yeah. The tin Kodgen. Did you know Black Baby? Brickley, they called him Black Baby? No. He had one of those bands around.
Yeah, they had a Washboard band.

Oh yeah. Old Red was about to play Kodgen around there. Who's Red? He stood back to the piano. He'd play the piano and drum and that Kodgen. Take a glass and Wawa's like that Kodgen. That's right. Make it sound like that trumpet. What happened to him? I don't know. I haven't seen so many.
The fellas died out so fast, you know.

And all you know is Red? Yes, sir. I saw that. He's a Red. Red. I always call Red. It's sharp. Did you get his favorites, Phil? No. I think we copied that card all right. Okay. I hate to put you on the spot, but... Not all of them. Some of them. Black Ben A. What about favorite trumpet players? Did he talk about who your Rambam's trumpet player would be?
Well, Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly, Walter Blue, Cuckoo.
Cuckoo, huh?
Yeah. Bob Anthony. Bob was a pretty good player. Bob was hard.
He never had no power or great lip, but I mean... He's good. He was a Navy band.
This boy, this boy. What I was telling you about on Parker Street, I was telling you, Joe Doyard?
Yeah, Joe was a good trumpet player.
Joe was a good trumpet player. And Rick Carr. Rick Carr used to be one of my trumpet players. And all that was good.
Joe Doyard was a good trumpet player.
He was good. So he just gave it up. And this boy, Billy Moran's son, he was a good bass player. So he just... Simon. Simon was good. I was talking with Simon and Eddie.
So Simon and Eddie both?
Yeah. Both of them was playing bass. One was playing bass and one was playing banjo.
No, Eddie played banjo. One of them. Well, they was good. John was on banjo too, wasn't he?
No, John was playing bass, I believe, wasn't he?
John played bass, Lawrence, I mean John and Lawrence played banjo and Simon and Eddie played bass.

He played the bass. Because he just give up. He's a presser now. Simon's a presser now. He's a good bass player. He was, they was good. Now that's how I used to work all with them, in between, you know. They'd come and get me. But I'd pick them out, you know. They'd pick me. And that just kept me going. And just like Howard.
What about trombone players in those times?
Well, trombone, Joe Petit, that one. He was good. He was one of the real good ones. Yeah, he was good. That Joe? Jack Cattle. Yeah, Jack Carey. Jack Carey was good.
Did you ever hear a guy called Henry Ford? I think he played guitar. I think he was from the Ninth Ward.
And uh, how'd it come?
Played with Ambrose Powers, you know, the trombone player?

Yeah. How'd it call him? How'd it call him? This is uh, Papa, how'd they call a lady with the Barry the other day, from Badamba Barrel, within the ward by mom in the hospital? Was Mary? No. I don't know him good. That boy was within the hospital. His mom was in the hospital right side, mama there. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Thomas Copeland. Thomas Copeland, you heard him?
He's a bass player. Yeah, he's good there, Copeland. Yeah, I played a long time.
Yeah, Thomas Copeland, good.

You played with him a long time, Nero? Yeah, I played Maurice Durand down there a long time. Maurice and all that? And he was the bass player and I was playing with the Olympia Suriners and all the pass. I remember he did that, and it all, but he didn't. Cam Wright started playing bass again. But he's dead now. Oh yeah. He's got a son just like him. What did Maurice Durand do on Carnival? Now you tell me about that. On Carnival we used to play the Arabian Packing Company parade. From the Seminart, right down there.
From the Seminart, right down there.
From the Seminart. The Seminart's pass. It's sad, but it's still going on. Yeah, they have that parade. Did you ever play it? No, I never played. You must have been with the Buzzards, huh?
I was with the Buzzards.
You had them long?
Oh, I've been with the Buzzards for years. They tried to get me to go back now. I don't know, I might go with the Buzzards next year if Harold don't have nothing. I ain't going to be there.
He ain't going to be there?
I'm not going to be there.

He came out there, he ain't going to be there. No, I'm not going to be playing for him. Oh. That's what I said. I'm not going to play for him. Not Carnival, huh? No, not Carnival. I'll be right around here at Carnival. I don't be playing a little short parade like the Zulu. Or maybe if I could land at the Arabian Packing Company, they'd be through at one o'clock in the day. What do you think about the Zulu parade? Do you like it or not? Yeah, I like it. I think it's been going on many years. You know when I was a kid, after I'd seen the Zulu and then see Rex, first I'd catch the Indians falling out the morning. Then I'd go catch the Zulus in the basin, and then I'd see Rex, that's when I had my Carnival. That's when I was around the neighborhood, with the baby dolls and all that would be passing all through the day. You really had maskers in them days. I mean, they had more masks than they had people unmasked.

Million dollar dolls. That's right. Them women would be masking, and all of them have a hundred dollar bills. Their whole leg around they're stopping. They may not put no hundred dollar bills in their legs now. Cut their legs off. Cut their legs off. I'd go and hear the music. He loves music. He can play a drum, yeah.
How old is he? Thirty-four.
Thirty-four. Thirty-five. Thirty-five.

And he likes this kind of music? Oh yeah. Probably he's down there way, because I'm going to touch you a little bit of bar. Well you've got some kids in your family that play with that saxophone player name. Oh yeah.
Oh that.

You remember the day when they were making the television movie around the world? The television movie around at the Jean Zanet? You brought a boy over there with you? I think he's your nephew or something. He plays music. You introduced me to this young guy. I know him, but I can't think of his name. I'm not doing it. I might just be a friend of yours. I don't know. I don't know.
My sister boy. That was my sister boy. Warren, isn't he? Warren. Oh yeah. He plays sax. He from Booker Teele School. What's your name, Warren's what?
Warren Glass. Did the white people follow Zulu in the old days when you were young? Oh, from the time I seen them, they used to come out and look.

That's all they look for now. They enjoy the night house. They enjoy the night house. They enjoy the night house. They enjoy the night house. They enjoy the night house. They always mixed it up there, huh? Yeah. They lighted that. See on that basin, man? You couldn't get around it. You couldn't get there.

People used to get there extra oil so they could not get close enough to see. And they'd give them coconuts, you know? They couldn't hardly get. And then they'd let them have sacks of coconut on there. But they used to let them destroy it. You know, they stop them from trying to destroy it. Yeah, I remember right there. Yeah, I guess somebody's lovely daughter or son might have got hit for it, I guess. That's right. They throw coconuts to you. When did they stop it, Bill? Oh, I think the last six or seven years. Yeah, this is probably . I see a lot of white people with coconut this year. Yeah, they can give it to them, they hand it to them. No choice, they hand it to them. It's a little green.
It's what kind of danger, though, if they throw a coconut, you would be looking, the bushing in there could kill you.
It's what kind of danger.
Well, the question is this, if you're throwing a coconut to a poison, this person

misses it, the other person gets hit with it. I mean, you can't condemn a parade for that, no. I mean, that's just one death, the tradition. I just wondered why they condemned, I cannot understand why they condemned the Zulus. I don't understand. I can't understand either, they've been going up about 40, 50 years. Yeah. And everybody seems to get out and have a good time together. Everybody have a lovely time. I'mma see if you can get Johnny Prados.
You ever have Johnny Prados get your house? No, I don't have. I'mma see all this.
I think it's Wooda. Glenny told me where his Wooda was and I could never find it.
Albert Glenny. Albert Glenny. You, you. That's on Villery Street over near St. Bernard. I'm running there.

The man thing right now you try to do is see if you can hook up and get that picture of Wooden Joe with Chris Kelly on. I'mma see for it. I'mma see for it. That's what we want. I'mma get it for you. That's what we want. That's the man thing right now. So if we can get a picture of Chris Kelly, that'd be something, you know? Chris Kelly and Buddy Petit? I guess I done asked every old musician. I'mma see for it.
What I know. You know how to have Chris Kelly's picture? He would got Ike. What I say? Big Ike would got his legs off. Big Ike?
Oh you mean big Ike.

Ike. He's got his two legs off. Both of them off though? Yeah, both of them was off. I don't think we have. Well, him and I, him and Chris stayed right close to each other. I know that. Yeah. I know that. And I'm more sure he might know where I can get my hand on it. Well, between him and, between him and Parker there. What's that lady? Parker there. Where the Parker?

What's that lady name you mentioned a while ago with Wooden Joe? Lulu. Lulu Pascal. Lulu Pascal. Lulu Pascal. Lulu Pascal, my name. She's old time bro. I'mma see for it. I think she's still there. I'mma see for it. She's old time bro. They ought to keep all that, you know? Yeah, I'mma see. This used to be my boy.
I'mma see if I can get that picture.
So those musicians, they didn't have many more. They didn't. They didn't.

That's all they had to be on the field. That's all they had to be on the field. That's all they had to do to be a musician. That's all. That's all you had to do. That would make me take a license to play music. Play this for your wife. I love that, no, I love that. He said that in front of them. Oh yeah. My wife knows the women love me. I like the women, but I do women's high and chill. You see them on that parade, eh? They be by me, don't they? They be by me. They be by me. They be by me. I be by them too. Well, how's it about, oh yeah, that's right, you said you play with the Suns thing? Yeah. Yeah, I play with Papa Suns thing. Yeah. I play with Papa Suns thing. Yeah. When you get here with the other people, you know the women's love me. I like the women's, but I do women's high and chill. You see them on that parade, eh? They be by me, don't they? They be by me, don't they? They be by me. They be by me. They be by me. They be by me too. Well, how's it about, oh yeah, that's right, you said you play with the Suns thing?

Yeah, I play with Papa Suns thing. Yeah. I play with the band, with Papa Suns thing. Did you get who was in Suns thing then? Did we get that? Well he said most of them. He said all the fellas would work together. Some think of the job he's bad, he's bad, he's bad, he's bad. Yeah.
That's why you call it Papa Suns thing, you know?
And he wouldn't have the steady men, huh?

No. Like Harold and me, he'd come get me. Well you see, before Papa Suns thing died, he wasn't along playing with me. I used to go get him. I don't know if you remember when he had his leg broke, he'd walk with his stick. But Papa, I used to go get him. Amen. I used to go get him and bring him home, that's why. He had a dog. And his wife had spent over a hundred dollars trying to kill that dog. And I went and killed that dog, went there one Sunday. That's the last time I was at his house. And I went there that Sunday and she was there with that dog. He had the stimpers. Huh? Huh? Huh? Huh? She said, I done spent over a hundred dollars for my dog. She said, trying to kill him. Had medicine. I didn't know what all it got about. Big bottle, little bottle. I said, that's all. I said, I can kill that dog before you go to the grocery. She said, oh, go with glass. I said, yeah. I said, I can kill that dog. I said, you got the medicine right in here. She didn't bleed me. Now you know what I done? Didn't do no more in the garden. I said, you give me some salt. Table salt? Took that table salt. Two big tablespoons for him. I said, he ain't gonna bite. She said, no, I'm gonna hold him. I caught that dog and I made a hole in him and I squeezed him between my legs, you know. And I caught his mouth and I opened it. And I poured that salt down in there. Rub it. Rub it till he swallowed it. See when I turned him loose? He done that and he swallowed it. That was all. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. He's cured. And the dog, you see what the stem is. Two tablespoons of salt. Two tablespoons.
Two tablespoons.

Two of them big tablespoons full of salt. Put it down his throat and rub it. You know what he gonna do? He gonna go around in the grass. He gonna take his nose and he gonna dig. He gonna dig a hole there and he go, ah. See when he do that? And the head coming up. So he gonna go, he just gonna run around. That salt is getting him. He gonna run all around. He come right back to that hole and dig what he knows.
You see?
